metadata.name: tr
metadata.description: Translate, squeeze, or delete characters from standard input

installation.note: tr is a built-in command available on all Linux systems by default

overview.summary: The tr (translate) command reads from standard input, translates or deletes characters, and writes to standard output. It's a simple but powerful tool for character-level text transformations. Unlike sed, tr works on individual characters, making it perfect for case conversion, character deletion, and character replacement.
when_to_use: Convert text to uppercase or lowercase
Replace one set of characters with another

syntax.description: Translate characters from SET1 to corresponding characters in SET2. If SET2 is omitted, characters in SET1 are deleted. Reads from stdin and writes to stdout.

options.description: Delete characters in SET1, do not translate
options.use_case: Remove specific characters from text, like removing all digits or punctuation

options.description: Replace sequence of characters with a single occurrence
options.use_case: Remove duplicate characters, like collapsing multiple spaces into one
Work with characters NOT in the set - delete everything except digits, for example

examples.title: Convert to uppercase
examples.description: Convert all lowercase letters to uppercase

output_explanation.format: All characters in first set replaced with corresponding characters in second set

elements.meaning: Source set: all lowercase letters from a to z
Target set: all uppercase letters from A to Z
Result: each lowercase letter replaced with its uppercase equivalent

output_explanation.notes: tr maps characters positionally: 'a'->'A', 'b'->'B', etc. Works character by character.

examples.use_case: Normalize text case, prepare data for case-sensitive operations

examples.title: Convert to lowercase
examples.description: Convert all uppercase letters to lowercase

output_explanation.format: Uppercase characters replaced with lowercase equivalents
output_explanation.notes: Reverse of uppercase conversion. Common for normalizing user input or file names.

examples.use_case: Normalize text to lowercase for consistent processing

examples.title: Delete specific characters

output_explanation.format: All characters in the specified set are removed

elements.meaning: Set of characters to delete (all digits)
Result: all digits removed, letters remain

output_explanation.notes: The -d flag deletes characters instead of translating them. Useful for cleaning data.

examples.use_case: Remove unwanted characters like digits, punctuation, or special characters

examples.title: Replace spaces with newlines
examples.description: Split text by spaces into separate lines

output_explanation.format: Each space character replaced with a newline character

elements.meaning: Result: each word on its own line

output_explanation.notes: Converts space-separated text into line-separated text. Useful for processing word lists.

examples.use_case: Split space-separated values into lines for line-by-line processing

examples.description: Replace multiple consecutive spaces with a single space

output_explanation.format: Sequences of the specified character are collapsed to a single occurrence

elements.meaning: Result: multiple spaces collapsed to one

output_explanation.notes: The -s flag collapses sequences. '    ' (4 spaces) becomes ' ' (1 space). Useful for cleaning whitespace.

examples.title: Delete everything except digits
examples.description: Keep only digits, delete all other characters

Result: only digits remain, all letters deleted

output_explanation.notes: Combining -c and -d: -cd means 'delete everything except this set'. Very useful for extracting specific character types.

examples.use_case: Extract only specific character types from mixed text (digits, letters, etc.)

misconceptions.title: tr works on words or lines
misconceptions.misconception: tr can replace words or work on entire lines like sed
misconceptions.reality: tr works only on individual characters, not words or lines. It's character-by-character translation, not pattern matching.
misconceptions.tip: Use sed for word/line replacements, tr for character-level operations

misconceptions.title: tr can edit files directly
misconceptions.misconception: tr can modify files in place like sed -i
misconceptions.reality: tr only reads from stdin and writes to stdout. To modify a file, use redirection: tr 'a-z' 'A-Z' < file.txt > output.txt
misconceptions.tip: Always use redirection or pipes with tr. It doesn't have an in-place edit option.

misconceptions.title: tr understands character classes like regex
misconceptions.misconception: tr can use regex character classes like [0-9] or \d
misconceptions.reality: tr uses simple character sets and ranges (a-z, 0-9), not regex. Use [:digit:], [:alpha:], etc. for POSIX character classes.

common_pitfalls.description: If SET1 and SET2 have different lengths, tr may not work as expected
common_pitfalls.solution: Ensure character sets match in length, or use character classes. For deletion, use -d with single set.

common_pitfalls.description: Special shell characters like *, ?, [ need proper quoting or escaping
common_pitfalls.solution: Always quote character sets: tr 'a-z' 'A-Z' not tr a-z A-Z. Use single quotes to prevent shell expansion.

common_pitfalls.description: Newlines (\n) need proper escaping and may behave differently
common_pitfalls.solution: Use '\n' in single quotes, or $'\n' for proper newline handling. Test with echo first.

related_commands.relationship: Text replacement; sed works on patterns/words, tr works on characters
related_commands.description: Stream editor for filtering and transforming text

related_commands.relationship: Text processing; awk is more powerful but tr is simpler for character operations
related_commands.description: Pattern scanning and text processing language

related_commands.relationship: Character extraction; cut extracts by position, tr transforms characters
related_commands.description: Remove sections from lines of files

best_practices: Always quote character sets to prevent shell expansion: tr 'a-z' 'A-Z'
Use POSIX character classes for portability: [:digit:], [:alpha:], [:space:]
Combine -s with other operations to clean text: tr -s ' ' to collapse spaces
Use -cd pattern to extract specific character types: tr -cd '0-9' keeps only digits
Test with echo first before applying to files: echo 'test' | tr 'a-z' 'A-Z'
performance_tips: tr is very fast for character-level operations, faster than sed for simple character translation
Works well in pipelines for streaming data processing
For very large files, tr is more efficient than sed for character operations

additional_notes.character_sets: tr uses character sets, not regex. Ranges like a-z, 0-9 are supported
additional_notes.stdin_only: tr only reads from stdin, never from files directly - always use pipes or redirection
additional_notes.no_inplace: tr cannot edit files in place - always redirect output to modify files
